item.title: Erectile Dysfunction After Prostate Surgery
item.description:
Sex

Erectile Dysfunction After Prostate Surgery

What to expect when recovering from a prostatectomy.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Nearly all men experience some erectile difficulty after prostate surgery, even with nerve-sparing technique.
  • Recovery is slow, occurring over a year or more. Not everyone returns to their baseline functioning.
  • Starting medication or a vacuum device soon after surgery might help preserve tissue health.

A prostate cancer diagnosis can be devastating. It brings us face-to-face with our mortality. Even knowing the high survival rates may not limit the worry and grief. While surgery can remove a tumor, it doesn’t always resolve the emotional impact of this experience. This is especially true when erectile difficulty occurs post-prostatectomy.

Please note the following case is a composite with client details anonymized to protect privacy.

Source: Yaroslav Shuraev / Pexels

Tom was 62 when a routine PSA test led to a prostate cancer diagnosis. He eventually had a nerve-sparing radical prostatectomy. By every clinical measure, the surgery was a success. However, three months later, Tom continued to experience severe post-operative erectile dysfunction (ED). His penis would not become erect with his partner or during masturbation.

He was informed of the risk to his sexual functioning before surgery. Even then, he was not fully prepared for the emotional experience of ED. The arousal that used to happen effortlessly now felt impossible. He mourned a loss of function, a loss of normalcy, and a loss of connection to his partner and his own sexuality.

This is one of the most common effects of prostate cancer treatment. It is not necessarily an indicator that something went wrong.

Why Erection Loss Happens

The nerves that control erections run alongside the prostate in bundles so fine that even the most skilled, nerve-sparing surgery can bruise, stretch, or inflame them. Nerve tissue heals slowly. In the meantime, this interferes with the signals that regulate blood flow and support erections.

Nearly all men will have some change in erectile function in the first few months after prostate surgery, regardless of how the procedure went. Although it is an expected part of recovery, it can still be a distressing experience, particularly when it is severe and occurs over an extended period of time.

Recovery of erectile function is typically slower to return than other bodily functions. Continence, for example, often returns within a few months post-surgery. Erections can sometimes have slow improvement over the course of a year or more.

The Reality of Recovery

Everyone's recovery is different. Some regain their previous level of functioning. Some may not return to baseline but do experience an improvement in their ED symptoms. Others may continue to experience severe dysfunction.

Several factors affect how much function returns and how quickly: the patient’s age, erectile functioning before surgery, the extent of nerve tissue damage, the presence of other health conditions like diabetes or cardiovascular disease, and if the patient is taking erectile medication.

Tom was healthy and had no other major risk factors. He also had a surgeon experienced in nerve-sparing technique. He still experienced a year with limited responsiveness and constant worry that he was irreparably changed. The surgery had been a clear solution to the problem of cancer. Addressing his sexual functioning felt more uncertain and prolonged.

Ask your surgeon before the procedure how much nerve-sparing is realistic and what a reasonable recovery timeline might look like for someone with your history. It won’t guarantee a particular outcome, but that conversation might help adjust your expectations.

Penile Rehabilitation

Many urologists recommend starting some form of penile rehabilitation soon after surgery, often as soon as the catheter comes out. The idea is that regular blood flow helps keep erectile tissue healthy while the nerves recover.

This typically means starting a low dose of a PDE-5 inhibitor (such as sildenafil, tadalafil, or avanafil) and using a vacuum erection device on a regular basis. Evidence for rehabilitation strategies is still being researched, but this strategy is usually recommended because the risks are low and the potential benefit is meaningful. While outcomes vary, men who use a PDE-5 inhibitor are more likely to experience a return to baseline.

If difficulty persists beyond a year or two of rehabilitation, there are other options. Injectable medication can produce a functional erection when oral medications aren’t effective. Penile implants have been shown to be a reliable and satisfying option for men who choose one.

Tom started with a daily PDE-5 inhibitor and a vacuum device. Some months felt like there was no change at all. After the first year, he looked back in hindsight and recognized an overall improvement had occurred. His erections were not always reliable and were not always firm enough for penetration, but, with the help of medication, intercourse became possible once again.

Resilience in Recovery

One of the hardest parts for many men post-prostatectomy is a split experience: being told you’re cured while noticing there's still a problem.

If you’re in the middle of this recovery, the timeline back to “normal” can feel indefinite or, at least, longer than expected. The recovery process can be unpredictable, but it is usually worth remaining consistent with the rehabilitation protocol past the point where it feels discouraging.

Sometimes, a new normal has to be defined.

Erectile function is not the same as libido, orgasm, or pleasure. Many men can still reach climax and ejaculation during recovery, even without a full erection. Noticing pleasure may require a different mindset but can still be accessible. These distinctions are easy to forget when experiencing the stress of erection loss.

Tom eventually stopped treating his erections as proof of normalcy. Once he backed away from that performance pressure, he found it easier to talk to his partner about what was happening. He continued with his rehab program without losing hope. Together, he and his partner began to pay more attention to the other ways their intimacy returned.

item.title: The Emergency Room Catches Teens at the Worst Moment
item.description:
Addiction

The Emergency Room Catches Teens at the Worst Moment

Drug screening rates in emergency rooms are high, but referral rates are not.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Screening rates for substance use are high but linkage to care is vey limited.
  • Substance-related emergency department visits among youth rose nearly 48 percent between 2016 and 2021.
  • Lower-income ZIP codes generate fewer pediatric opioid EMS calls but higher rates of naloxone use.

A 16-year-old comes into the emergency department after a night that went sideways. Maybe it's a car crash. Maybe it's a panic attack that won't stop, or a friend who called 911 because someone wasn't breathing right. The chief complaint rarely says "substance use." It says something else. Somewhere in that visit, a screening question gets asked, and the answer changes what should happen next.

In our ED, that question has been asked of adolescent ED patients for over 12 years, with completion rates above 92 percent. Screening was never where things fell apart.

Where Things Fall Apart

A positive screen gets written into a provider note 57 percent of the time. It shows up in the assessment and plan, the section that actually drives discharge decisions, in just 9 percent of encounters. A referral to treatment gets documented in fewer than 1 percent. In one review of 743 adolescents who screened positive at our ED, three encounters had a documented referral, and none of those three had documented follow-up care. Zero.

Nationally, the pattern repeats. Fewer than one in five adolescents with a substance use disorder gets any treatment. Fewer than a third get follow-up care within 60 days of an ED visit where substance use came up. One in five returns to the ED within a year for a substance-related visit. The door keeps swinging, and almost nobody walks through the other one, into care.

The ED is often the only point of contact these teens have with the health system for this issue. They don't seek out primary care for substance use on their own, and parents don't always know what to ask a pediatrician. The ED sees adolescents at 2 a.m., in crisis, when the walls are down and honesty comes easier than it does at a scheduled 15-minute well visit. That window closes fast.

Prehospital data tell a related story. In a statewide analysis of pediatric opioid EMS encounters, higher-income ZIP codes generated more calls than lower-income ones, but in lower-income areas, when EMS did respond, naloxone got administered at a higher rate. It says something about who gets noticed and who gets treated once someone finally shows up.

We started a peer recovery navigator program at our ED two years ago. It's still small. The adolescents enrolled in it are the first cohort in our system's history to get anyone checking in on them after that ED door swings shut behind them.

item.title: Respect Is the Emotional Currency of Success
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Respect Is the Emotional Currency of Success

How everyday interactions shape trust, confidence, and who we become.

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • Every interaction is an emotional exchange—a deposit or withdrawal.
  • "Reliable respect" creates reserves that help us navigate difficult moments.
  • Repeated disrespect can become so familiar that we stop recognizing its impact.

Disrespect can change us more than we realize.

Sometimes it’s obvious. Other times it happens in moments that seem too small to matter—being repeatedly interrupted before we finish a thought, having an idea dismissed without consideration, or realizing that our perspective was requested but never really valued. We may become a little less likely to speak the next time or a little more cautious about offering an idea. We may even begin to question whether what we have to contribute matters.

Source: Monkey Business Images / Shutterstock

The opposite can happen, too—a teacher who believes in us at precisely the right moment, a colleague or leader who takes the time to listen, or someone who sees potential in us when we are struggling to see it ourselves. Each of these moments may seem ordinary, yet each can influence what happens next, and over time, who we become.

Through my experiences, I have become increasingly curious about what shapes these moments and what happens next. It's a question I've explored in my work and in my TEDx talk, "The Ripple Effect of Respect." In operating rooms, classrooms, boardrooms, and everyday life, I've noticed how small interactions shape the emotional climate around us, how willing people are to engage, and what they feel able to contribute, particularly when moments of respect—or disrespect—are repeated and become so familiar that we no longer recognize their impact.

Beyond Status and Accomplishments

“Respect” is a word we use in many ways. We may respect someone because of what they have accomplished—their expertise, position, or achievements. We may respect someone because we admire how they live or conduct themselves. Respect can also mean recognizing authority, honouring another person's boundaries, or simply giving someone the space that belongs to them.

The respect I'm referring to here, however, is more fundamental. It doesn't need to be earned through accomplishment, position, or status. It begins with acknowledging another person's inherent dignity and allowing that recognition to shape how we treat them. It is the respect that says, “You have value because you are here. Your experiences may be different from mine. Your perspective may challenge mine. I may not even agree with you. But you are still worthy of being seen, heard, and thoughtfully considered.”

This kind of respect lives less in what we say we believe, and more in the ordinary moments between us. It doesn't require agreement. In many ways, its presence becomes most meaningful when we disagree. Moments like allowing someone to finish a thought before we respond, listening because we are genuinely interested rather than waiting for our turn to speak, or considering an idea before dismissing it may seem insignificant, yet together they accumulate and help create environments in which people either thrive or eventually disengage.

article continues after advertisement

Workplace Trends

In 2025, Gallup reported that only 37 percent of U.S. employees strongly agreed that they were treated with respect at work, returning to a record low first measured in 2022. In a separate national survey, Pew Research Center found that 57 percent of workers who voluntarily left a job in 2021 said that feeling disrespected at work was one reason they quit. Findings like these reinforce something I had already been observing across medicine, education, leadership, and everyday life, observations that shaped my philosophy, which has become central to my work:

Respect is the emotional currency of success.

Currency has value because it enables exchange. To me, respect functions similarly—every interaction is an emotional exchange. We make deposits or withdrawals in one another's emotional reserves. When we listen with genuine curiosity, consider someone's perspective, or hold someone accountable without diminishing them, we make a deposit. When we dismiss, interrupt, belittle, or disregard them, we make a withdrawal.

And like any reserve, what has accumulated matters.

"Reliable Respect"

While one respectful moment certainly matters, it's the consistency that shapes us most deeply. When people experience respect reliably, including during disagreements, it can create a sense of safety that allows for honesty, learning, and growth. That consistency builds what I have coined reliable respect. It creates reserves we can draw on when things are difficult.

The opposite is also true. When those reserves have been depleted by repeated disrespect, a single interaction can carry far more weight than it might otherwise. A dismissive word at the wrong time can be enough for someone to stop speaking up, walk away from an opportunity, or begin to imagine a different path. And when that happens at a critical point in someone’s journey, what is lost may extend far beyond the interaction itself—the confidence, contribution, or possibility that might otherwise have followed.

article continues after advertisement

There are times when self-respect requires us to notice what we have been accepting. There are other times when it asks us to look honestly at what we may be contributing. None of us moves through our relationships without occasionally interrupting, dismissing, becoming impatient, or getting something wrong. I know I don’t. Perhaps what matters is whether we notice, and what we do next.

Lately, I've found myself asking a simple question after many of my own interactions:

What kind of exchange just took place?

Did I add something to another person's emotional reserve, or take something away? What did they leave with? What did I? And if we were to look at the balance created by our interactions over time, what might we find?

We move through dozens of these exchanges every day, often without giving them much thought.

I wonder what we might notice if we started paying attention.

Copyright Nina Ahuja, MD

item.title: How to Give a Great Compliment
item.description:
Relationships

How to Give a Great Compliment

Are your words landing the way you intend them to?

Posted August 11, 2026

Key points
  • A compliment can brighten someone's day, yet we tend to withhold them.
  • Studies suggest people appreciate compliments more than we realize.
  • Giving compliments can be an art, although an easy one to learn.
  • Why not be generous with your words to help others feel seen?
Source: Jill Wellington/Pixabay

Everyone loves compliments. They help make us feel seen and appreciated for who we are. Whatever your role (parent, partner, friend, colleague), you are in a unique position to make those around you feel better about themselves. In my 20 years as a psychologist, I have learned some important strategies for giving compliments that are both effective and informed by science. Happy complimenting!

Be specific. Research suggests that the more specific a compliment, the better it makes the receiver feel. Telling your partner that you like their shirt is nice. Adding that they look handsome in that shirt means even more. If you really want to bring it home, mention that they look handsome in that shirt and it brings out their beautiful blue eyes. Wow, that one will really land, trust me.

Be genuine. This one sounds obvious, but I imagine we have experienced instances when we felt “buttered up.” This might apply more to the workplace when someone is trying to curry favor (i.e., brown-nose). An insincere compliment is worse than no compliment at all, so I encourage you to always be genuine when giving a compliment. If you look hard enough, there is almost always something flattering to mention anyway, so identify those good qualities. A bonus? Compliment-givers tend to feel better afterward, even if they were anxious about speaking up in the first place.

Be generous. Ironically, studies suggest we underestimate how good our compliments will make others feel and overestimate how uncomfortable a compliment might make them. So, we hold back. The world is difficult, and a small compliment goes a long way to building goodwill. I am writing this post from an airplane, and ironically, a flight attendant just complimented my pants (shout out to Frontier Airlines). That small gesture made me feel seen and also made me want to return the compliment by mentioning the airline. Compliments can start a virtuous cycle that ends with lots of people feeling good.

If you are a parent, compliments take on additional importance. Your children really look up to you. They wish to please you. It means the whole world to them if you see them clearly and like what you see. That is why you will want your compliments to check all the boxes above. If you say, “You’re a good kid,” that is really nice. If you say, “I saw how kind you were to that little boy on the playground when he slipped,” that will really resonate.

We all want to be seen and appreciated for who we are, deep down. I don’t care if you are 8 or 80 years old. It feels good when others see our positive qualities. Please do not be stingy with your compliments. It will make those around you feel happier, and it will boost your mood as well!
